prompt: A Linux database server keeps 40 GiB of hot table files in the page cache. Every night a backup job reads 500 GiB of other files once, sequentially. With the classic active/inactive LRU design, which design feature can help protect hot pages against a one-pass scan?

options.text: The backup bypasses the page cache automatically because it reads sequentially
options.explanation: Normal buffered reads go through the page cache regardless of pattern. Only `O_DIRECT` or `posix_fadvise` hints change that.

options.text: Inactive admission and promotion based on observed reuse can reduce one-pass scan pollution. Hot active pages can be better protected, though refault handling and memory pressure add exceptions
options.explanation: Correct as a simplified description of scan-resistant admission. Exact promotion depends on observed references, refault history and the kernel; active pages can still be reclaimed under pressure.

options.text: The kernel uses OPT for file pages because it can predict sequential reads
options.explanation: Readahead predicts what to load next, not when pages will be reused. OPT remains unimplementable.

options.text: kswapd never reclaims page-cache pages that belong to a database
options.explanation: The kernel does not know or care which program owns a page-cache page. Hot pages survive because of how they are ranked, not who owns them.

workedExample: Inactive admission and reuse-based promotion reduce pollution compared with pure LRU, but do not guarantee that 40 GiB of hot data survives a 500 GiB scan. Reclaim scope, capacity and kernel policy matter. POSIX_FADV_DONTNEED can advise dropping already-cached file data; it does not bypass the cache in the way suitable O_DIRECT I/O can. Hints and direct-I/O alignment/support requirements must be checked.

link.title: Page Frame Reclamation — Understanding the Linux VMM

prompt: A latency-sensitive service on Linux shows occasional 50 ms stalls inside `malloc` and page faults, at times when `free` shows little free memory but lots of cache. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: An allocation that cannot obtain suitable pages may enter direct reclaim when its allocation flags allow it, stalling the allocating task
options.explanation: Correct. Direct reclaim executes in the allocating context, but flags, cgroup pressure, order and fragmentation determine whether it runs.

options.text: kswapd starts reclaiming when free memory drops below the low watermark and stops when it reaches the high watermark
options.explanation: Correct. kswapd is the background reclaimer. Raising the gap between watermarks gives it more room to stay ahead.

options.text: Raising `vm.min_free_kbytes` or `vm.watermark_scale_factor` can make kswapd start earlier and reduce direct reclaim
options.explanation: Correct. Higher watermarks wake kswapd sooner, at the cost of keeping more RAM idle.

options.text: Low 'free' memory with lots of cache proves the machine is thrashing
options.explanation: Incorrect. Linux deliberately fills RAM with cache. Thrashing shows up as high fault and swap rates or high memory PSI, not low free memory alone.

options.text: `/proc/pressure/memory` can show whether tasks are actually stalling on memory
options.explanation: Correct. PSI's `some` and `full` lines report the share of time tasks were blocked on memory reclaim or refaults.

workedExample: Watermarks influence background reclaim and allocation reserves, while cgroup limits and allocation constraints can also cause direct reclaim. Correlate stalls with reclaim/compaction tracing and memory PSI; a 50 ms duration alone does not establish the cause. Watermark tuning may help at a capacity cost but is not a universal fix. Free memory alone is insufficient; inspect MemAvailable, cgroup usage and pressure.
